235.t: Playing with Coleman Hawkins on 52nd Street and his habits
235.s: Dressed and moustached like Hawkins, he sat in with him, and learned from his handmade clothes, new car every year and fresh horns; Nicholas got his own car only in 1954.
235.ch: Back in New York: Heard and Dizzy
235.q: : Yes, well everybody knew he was my idol and I dressed like him, I played like him and I had a moustache like him. And, you know, I was there all the time. So one night he said, "I think I'll play 'Body and Soul' in E natural." So I says, "O.K.". And we played it and he laughed and he said, after…

235.t: Tenor models on the radio: Herschel, Chu, Lester, Ben
235.s: As a student he wanted a sound and listened to Herschel Evans, Chu Berry, Lester Young, Dick Wilson and Ben Webster.
235.q: : Well, even way back then I realized that I wanted to have a sound, because...listening to Herschel, listening to Ben and I heard some things by Coleman Hawkins in a music store...and I wasn't aware of him, because I'd heard Chu Berry and I loved him. And I became involved in sound. Chu Berry and,…

235.t: Hearing Chu Berry, Ben Webster and Hawkins and the big sound
235.s: Asked how he got a big tenor sound, he compares Chu's fluid tone, Ben Webster's taste and Coleman Hawkins's bigger tone.
235.ch: First jobs and finding his sound
235.q: Well, I'll tell you, I was impressed with Chu, he had a fluid sound. I used to catch Cab Calloway from the Cotton Club, on the radio, and he had a fluid sound. Now I'm gonna tell you how this thing affected me. I says "Well!", 'cause nobody played no faster than Chu, you know, he was fast.

235.t: Breathing, Ben in Lansing and meeting Coleman Hawkins in Chicago
235.s: He studied breathing, met Ben Webster in Lansing, and in 1941 heard Hawkins at Dave's Cafe in Chicago, where Hawkins taught him about sound and living well.
235.ch: First jobs and finding his sound
235.q: Then when Coleman Hawkins came back from Europe and he did "Body and Soul" and with that subdued...and so I said, "There's another dimension." But it was heavy and deep and that meant that you had to have control. So then I started learning my breathing exercises and I became aware of my health,…

235.t: Mid-1940s idols: Coleman Hawkins, Don Byas and Ben Webster
235.s: He explains what he most admired in Hawkins, Don Byas and Ben Webster at the time.
235.ch: Back in New York: Heard and Dizzy
235.q: Well Coleman Hawkins, mainly, because he seemed to have everything. All of his notes were clear and beautiful and he had an evenness about his horn and then his brain, he seemed to have such a deep knowledge of sound and chord structure and he just seemed to have everything. And he was actually…

235.t: Wanting the best: Hawkins's example and the Mercedes
235.s: He patterned his life on Hawkins and Ben Webster and wanted a Mercedes.
235.ch: First jobs and finding his sound
235.q: Yeah, well, you know I've always wanted the best in life that I could, you know, because you know I learned from Coleman...because when you see Ben Webster, he was always sharp. They always had the best saxophones in the world and they always sounded so beautiful. So I patterned my life like that,…

7.t: Coleman Hawkins' styles and Benny Carter's influence
7.s: Thomas argues Benny Carter influenced Hawkins' melodic turn and describes Hawkins as the man who made tenor saxophone respectable.
7.ch: Arrangers, Bill Robinson and Coleman Hawkins
7.q: And another thing I got on my mind (but my friend don't agree with me), I definitely think that Benny Carter had a great influence on Coleman Hawkins. Now, Coleman Hawkins may not admit it. Benny Carter sure won't admit it; he's such a great musician, he'll just brag about what a great musician…

7.t: Hawkins at a 52nd Street club; his friendship; Benny Carter's talent
7.s: Thomas asks Hawkins to play 'Body and Soul' on 52nd Street, notes the money-minded Hawkins, and praises Benny Carter's natural writing.
7.ch: Arrangers, Bill Robinson and Coleman Hawkins
7.q: But he was beautiful... And I went to one of the clubs on 52nd Street one night. That's when "Body and Soul" was popular. So I requested it. I said, "Coleman, would you play 'Body and Soul" for me?" He said, "Yeah." So he played it. And after he got... See, in them days I knew the so myself…

7.t: Hawkins' return from Europe and 'Body and Soul'
7.s: Thomas describes musicians dismissing Hawkins after Europe and his answer with 'Body and Soul', a solo modulating through three keys.
7.ch: Arrangers, Bill Robinson and Coleman Hawkins
7.q: It's the most... For a Jazz solo, it's the most accurate Jazz solo ever written. Because the miraculous thing he did, it changes keys three times. And he modulated into each change of key. And he almost had to have planned that solo before. Because he started out... [SINGS]...started out with the…

7.t: Staying in Coleman Hawkins' mother's house in St. Joe
7.s: As a school basketball player Thomas stayed in Hawkins' family house in St. Joseph and learned Hawkins started on cello.
7.ch: Arrangers, Bill Robinson and Coleman Hawkins
7.q: Yes. See, I knew Coleman personally, because I used to take... A lot of times when we had a contract for Coleman, I used to take the contracts up to his house to get him to sign, and he'd sign them, and I'd take them back to the office the next day. But I just idolized Coleman Hawkins, because man,…

7.t: Recording four tunes for Joe Davis with Coleman Hawkins
7.s: Thomas hires Hawkins for a hundred dollars a day, writes progressions for four tunes, and finds he reads the piano part.
7.ch: Arrangers, Bill Robinson and Coleman Hawkins
7.q: said, "Well, I'll check it out." So I called Coleman. I said, "Coleman, would you do a recording date with me?' He said, "Yeah." I said, "How much you want?" He said, "I'll do it for a hundred dollars a day." Well, that was so cheap, I think I told him "yeah" then. I didn't even check with Joe…

406.t: Coleman Hawkins's refusal to look back, and his love of argument
406.s: Hawkins insisted he never played slap-tongue solos, even when Barefield brought a Henderson record. Barefield describes him as loving musical arguments and being a fine reader, writer and pianist.
406.q: And the funny thing about it, Hawkins never liked to look back at things, you know. So we used to do an arrangement on -- I was only playing clarinet then, by the way, because we had Hawk and myself and I forget who was playing trumpet at that time. So we were doing -- did the St. Louis Blues. And…

406.t: From Trumbauer to Benny Carter as his alto idol
406.s: He had not yet met Hawkins in person; he switched his model to Benny Carter, whom he still calls the greatest all-round alto player and the creator of lead-alto style.
406.ch: Moten band, Kansas City and the evolution of jazz
406.q: I hadn't seen my idol yet, you know. But in the meantime I picked up on Benny Carter who I felt was the greatest alto player, you know. Because then I started thinking I liked Benny Carter. I started to try to play him, emulate, you know, tried to pick up his style of playing because after him, I…

406.t: What influenced Hawkins and Don Byas copying Tatum's solos
406.s: Asked about influences on Hawkins, Barefield says Benny Carter smoothed his rough style, and Byas learned his harmonic education by copying Tatum's records.
406.q: one of the things, if you listen to Fletcher's records, and the big things that influenced Hawk all of them was Benny Carter. See, before Benny Carter came with Fletcher Henderson, Hawk was a rough tenor player. He played -- his style that he played, though, was very, very rough.

0.t: Hawkins as master of the tenor, with Caldwell and Prince Robinson
0.s: Among early tenor players the three to get by were Hawk, Happy and Prince Robinson; Hawkins was master of slap tongue before dropping it.
0.ch: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
0.q: Yeah, because (unintelligible) when they'd say tenor players, they'd say Hawk, here (unintelligible), it was Hawk, Happy and Big Prince Robinson. So them were the three you had to get by because Bean was the master. We all called Hawk the master. That's what he was.

0.t: Drinks with Coleman Hawkins at the White Rose on 52nd Street
0.s: Hawkins, who never bought drinks for others, bought Caldwell drinks and urged him to keep his own style.
0.ch: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
0.q: Because I know when he was down in 52nd Street before the war, I used to go down there and catch him. So the place called the White Rose, and all of these (unintelligible) 52nd Street would hang playing (unintelligible) in there, and I'd go down (I went up to Ben Webster) there to catch Hawk, and I…

0.t: Who influenced whom among early tenors: Hawk, Happy and Prince Robinson
0.s: Everyone heard Hawk first; Prince Robinson started at the Calvert Palace and was influenced by Hawk.
0.q: You had to get -- got to get by all three of us. That was the whole question, tough thing. They made it that way. Whenever Hawk and I would be playing, we wouldn't pay that no mind, but that was the proving grounds.

124.t: Coleman Hawkins's "Body and Soul" and selling it in Boston
124.s: McRae recalls Hawkins's letter and buys 500 copies for Harvard students while Hawkins was in Europe; Welburn corrects the dating.
124.ch: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
124.q: Because Coleman say -- I understand somebody said to me that -- I got a letter from Coleman Hawkins. Coleman say, 'You guys say everybody say (inaudible) he's going back. But he's going to send you a little message to let you know that he's not going back,' you know. They figured Coleman had been…

124.s: McRae recalls musicians as dignified, well-dressed men, such as Coleman Hawkins strolling on 7th Avenue.
124.ch: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
124.q: Very clean gentleman. Most of the musicians that you are reading about or talking about, these fellows were just like -- (inaudible) just like doctors. They carried theirself as gentleman -- you know, musicians back there. Thought very highly of themselves. If we went out in the afternoons Hampton,…

124.t: Coleman Hawkins and the Selmer advertisements
124.s: Selmer's pictures of Hawkins with a gold Selmer drove McRae and many tenor players to switch; Hawkins visited the Savoy.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: Selmer gave Coleman Hawkins a horn, a gold horn, he told me. And they used his picture -- Coleman Hawkins playing the Selmer.

455.s: Budd recalls meeting Chu Berry in Chicago, describes his Hawkins-derived style, and Roy Eldridge's love of Hawkins and Armstrong records.
455.q: time I ever met Chu Berry he came to Chicago with Fletcher Henderson, and him and Roy Eldridge was boon coons -- they was runnin' around and we -- we used to go --

455.s: Budd rates Benny Carter among the greatest altos and tells a story of Phil Harris saying Carter scored his wife's films and played parts for the men.
455.q: Carter, they called him King, the King, because -- I'll tell you a little story about this. I had never heard nobody in the world playing alto saxiphone like Benny Carter, and he had such a beautiful, beautiful, fluid, flowing style. And so one day, you know, like when Billy Eckstine was trying to…

455.s: Budd praises Prince Robinson as nearly equal to Hawkins and recalls Clyde Hart copying his solo on 'Zonky'.
455.q: Oh, Prince Robertson, man! Prince Robertson, now he was running Coleman Hawkins a tight fight, because the cats were debating -- when I first heard of Prince Robertson was McKinney Cottonpickers-- I said, who is th is cat? Because he was sounding as great as Coleman Hawkins to me, almost, because…

1.s: Danny teased Steele that Hawkins was in town, and Steele told everybody at the Rhythm Club.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: Yeah, he respected musicians. He would respect everybody. I used to bug... I bugged him once. I said... He was crazy about Hawk. "Who was the greatest?" And he'd talk about the greatness... He was his idol. He worshipped...idol...idolized...

1.t: David Jones changes Coleman Hawkins's saxophone style
1.s: With the Missourians at the Savoy, Jones stopped New York saxophonists slap-tonguing and Hawkins came to hear him, which White links to Armstrong's chord use.
1.ch: Second session: family, Armstrong and David Jones
1.q: That’s what they used to do. You would do more of that than you done variations. David Jones didn’t come there with no slap tongue. David Jones run the changes all over the place. There were all the saxophones. Coleman Hawkins was the star in New York, because he was doing the [“cluck cluck cluck”…

85.t: Coleman Hawkins as a man and player, and the rivalry that was not
85.s: Carter sat beside Hawkins in Henderson's band, found him private and likeable, and sees no rivalry in Europe.
85.q: Well, I don’t know whether I can tell you too much about Coleman Hawkins, although we sat side by side in the Henderson Orchestra for quite a long while. How well we got to know each other is something else. He was pretty much of a private person—I guess that’s the term they use, you know—and you…

85.s: Carter says he found musicians by being on the scene, and describes Chu Berry as like Hawkins but with his own voice.
85.q: No. You just became aware of people by being on the scene. You hear them in some setting, or you hear of them and then you hear them. But this much later, I can’t say how or when, you know, I met or heard any of these particular guys, other than Coleman Hawkins, whom I heard, gee, about 1923 with…

953.t: Choosing Coleman Hawkins, and the hit 'Body and Soul'
953.s: Rollins says Hawkins was his idol and the epitome of the saxophone, and discusses the impact of 'Body and Soul' and Monk's question about it.
953.q: Well, I started with Louis Jordan, as we’ve been through. Um, my idol was Coleman Hawkins, because that was the person that, uh...I was, I gravitated to him. He was really the man, you know. And uh...

953.t: Why the 'Body and Soul' solo was so hard and why it broke through
953.s: He explains the technical and harmonic difficulty of Hawkins's solo and wonders why it became the hit.
953.q: Well, that was a hard solo. It was, um...they had transcriptions of it. They had everything of it. People we’re trying to play that, you know. I played some of it, but it was a difficult solo to really get. I don’t think I ever played the whole solo, you know.

68.t: Coleman Hawkins and the effect of Stampede
68.s: The Hawkins solo on Fletcher Henderson's Stampede eclipsed all other tenor players for Tate's generation.
68.q: Well, it was like -- I don't know, he was swinging so on "Stampede" and it was a terrific arrangement of Fletcher's in the first place. Everything was right there. And I'll never forget, it was in A flat and they played clarinets and it was just a hell of an arrangement, you know, absolutely…

68.t: Influence of Lester Young, Illinois Jacquet and Scott Hamilton
68.s: Tate says Jacquet inspired him to play more than Prez, and that Hamilton does too.
68.q: Yeah, he really did. Actually, he did a lot of things -- he made me always -- made me want to play. But Jacquet- I got more Jacquet - playing with Jacq', I got more vibes for one to play when he was in the band than I did with Prez. Because when Jacq' came in the band, man, he was really -- he was…

28.t: Melody Maker headline and the Hawkins-Carter jam at Aikian's club
28.s: Butler tells how Coleman Hawkins disliked a Dutch headline about his fall, and of the Czech saxophonist Andre Aikian's club, where Benny Carter pulled out a tenor to irk Hawkins.
28.ch: Reflections on Paris guitarists and saxophonists
28.q: And that's what was happening. And -- oh, of course, me and Patterson, that was the golden days. They had at one time the Melody Maker, which was an English newspaper of jazz. They says, the rise and fall of King Coleman Hawkins. And Benny Carter -- Coleman Hawkins happened to be in town and Benny…

28.t: Hawkins blows Honeysuckle Rose and wins over Pigalle
28.s: Hawkins, fortified with cognac, played Honeysuckle Rose until the whole of Pigalle crowded around, and Butler predicted he would surprise America.
28.ch: Reflections on Paris guitarists and saxophonists
28.q: -- Napoleon -- you don't feel it. You just feel good and Hawkins was building those castles and things -- and he was blowing and his little dog come right where he was and stood up and looked at Coleman Hawkins and then jumped up on the table.

103.t: Garvin Bushell, who first took Coleman Hawkins out on the road
103.s: Hinton praises Garvin Bushell; Jones says he was Coleman Hawkins's guardian when Hawkins first left home, and that their mothers knew each other.
103.q: was the cause of Coleman Hawkins [St. Joseph] first leaving his home in St. Joe, Missouri. Milt, there's something that very few people know. Coleman Hawkins had a ring and I had a ring, and I still have it. His mother and my mother in Omaha, Nebraska, Mrs. Louise Kelly, were friends.

103.t: Jesse Stone's band and Coleman Hawkins in Kansas City
103.s: He mentions Jesse Stone's 17-piece band and recalls that Coleman Hawkins's family required a guardian to travel with him.
103.q: He had 17 pieces. That's where Coleman Hawkins was worked after what's-his-name got him, after (Vincent) Gavin Bushell, San Juan... He was Coleman Hawkin's guardian because he could not leave home. Coleman could not leave home because the parents said, "You gotta." That's the way they did us, Milt.…

402.t: Who started the tenor sax style
402.s: Talk about early tenor players: Coleman Hawkins with Don Redman, Eddie Powers, Charlie Cordella and Lester Nelson.
402.q: I know what you mean. Well, I'll tell you, the first one I heard play like that was, a lot of people think, was Bostick, you know Bostick. Mm-hmm. Which, Samuel Terracopp's from Bostick. Mm-hmm. But the first guy I thought playing like that was a fella, maybe Armour could tell you that, too. I was…

770.s: Ayrton played almost identically to Rappolo.
770.q: Just like Rapolo. Just like Rapolo. They were almost identical. Very, very good.

431.t: Saxophone idols such as Coleman Hawkins
431.s: Hawkins was the early idol of saxophonists; the block degrades into repeated garbage text.
431.q: It was the earliest I can remember when people looked up to Coleman Hawkins. That early, huh? Yes, sir. When he was playing with Fletcher Henderson. And I mean real early, I'd say, when he was playing with Fletcher Henderson. So many of the American musicians started to date Coleman from the time…

39.t: Coleman Hawkins arriving in Chicago and as a creator
39.s: Brown recalls Hawkins coming to Chicago, possibly earlier with Mamie Smith, and calls him the number one saxophonist and a creator like Louis and Duke.
39.q: Well he just came here with Fletcher's band. Well I think he was here even earlier maybe with Mamey Smith. Yes he did, he used to be a violin player. Years ago he started on violin, that's why he got to be a saxophone player. He came here with Mamey Smith and played in the grand theater.

689.t: Coleman Hawkins and Bigard, and the need to read music in Chicago
689.s: A story of Bigard backing out of a contest with Coleman Hawkins after hearing him practice, and a remark that New Orleans musicians had to read in Chicago.
689.q: I said, well, they're two brothers, they're together. I said, I can't stop him. I don't give him. But he could have went the next day. Because if he just said, yeah, you want to go, I wouldn't accept for two weeks. I said, go on. I let him go. It's like going on Hawkins. You know what that band New…

780.t: Recording live in one take; David Lastie's sax solo
780.s: He sang and played piano live in one take; David Lastie took the solo and now plays with Frogman Henry.
780.q: I haven't heard him play lately. That's with Frogman Henry now. Yeah. I've heard him about maybe seven, eight months, something like that. I haven't heard him play lately. That's because I know him and I see him quite often. But I haven't heard him play in a little while.

298.t: Saxophone idols: Hodges and Bechet, and a New Orleans tenor with Basie
298.s: His sax idol was Johnny Hodges; talk turns to Bechet, whom he never knew, and to a New Orleans tenor man who played with Basie.
298.q: Yeah, you never did know him though, huh? Bechet? Yeah. No, Cindy Bechet. Yeah. No, I think he left there before I even got a teenager. I guess. Yeah. Well, you knew his brother, I guess. Yeah. Leonard. Yeah, I knew his brother. Yeah, I knew his brother. Just like Big O, I didn't know about him,…

805.t: Coltrane in the line from Hawkins, Lester Young and Parker
805.s: Asked about Coltrane, Cobb places him in a line of innovators from Coleman Hawkins to Lester Young and Parker.
805.q: Well you know it’s the same thing as what happened with — it’s a person like that comes maybe every so often, you know, that really changes the whole thing around. Like a long time ago I remember, you know, from where I’m starting, I’m starting like from maybe from Coleman Hawkins. But I’m sure…

809.t: Describing his own playing and early influences
809.s: Prez, Getz, Mulligan, Rollins, Coltrane and Johnny Hodges shaped his sound.
809.q: Well my playing comes from — the earliest references that I referenced were basically Gerry Mulligan, Prez, Stan Getz, Sonny Rollins, Coltrane. I mean I listened to all those guys. Lester Young was a huge influence on me and even to this day, I went through all the periods of music listening to…

954.t: Naming Sonny Rollins and Hank Mobley as influences
954.s: Asked whom he sounds like, LaLama picks Rollins and Mobley; Rowe liked the Mobley tune opening the concert.
954.q: I would probably have to say Sonny Rollins and Hank Mobley.

581.t: Calling him Bean, Benny Carter, and Hawkins teaching him chords
581.s: Locke's close friendship with Hawkins, Time magazine calling him after Hawkins died, and Hawkins pushing him to learn chordal Chopin pieces.
581.q: Yeah, well he was more than a friend. I mean like I said I was so close to those two guys for somebody my age. When he died, Time magazine called me up. And you know what they said? You know who told us to call you? We couldn’t believe it, because we called Benny Carter to ask him something about…

1003.t: Reviewing Hawkins's 'Body and Soul' with 'virgin ears'
1003.s: Rowe's curveball: how he would review the 1930s Hawkins record; he would find a metaphor, compare influences and consider the rhythm section.
1003.q: Okay? So now I’m just doing a stream of consciousness, okay? Johnny Green went to Harvard, okay? He’s a very, very well educated person. Maybe there’s something there, all right, that can lead me into describing, at least initially, as an entree into this revolutionary recording. Okay? The other…

554.t: Saxophone influences and Mingus calling him best jazz flutist
554.s: Hubert Laws and Joe Farrell are listened to, but Parker, Getz and Konitz influenced him most; Mingus and Mariano praised him.
554.q: I listen to a lot of the people like Hubert Laws and Joe Farrell. In fact most of my influence has been more like saxophone players you see. So that’s why I associate the bebop thing and the style plus my own whatever I do with those influences. So it seems like I listen to more saxophone players…

595.s: Pell played like Coleman Hawkins and Ben Webster as a teen, then turned to Lester Young's sound like Zoot and Stan.
595.ch: Lester Young and the Prez Conference
595.q: I think I played like Coleman Hawkins when I was in my 13 and 14 and 15 year old “Body and Soul,” that kind of thing, and Ben Webster. And then all of a sudden, this other sound came about with Zoot and Stan and some of the guys who were playing and they were playing like Lester. And I started…

360.t: Early listening and tone: Henderson, Ellington, Webster, Otto Link
360.s: He heard Henderson, Duke, Fats Waller, Hawkins and Webster, met Ben, and recalls his small-combo recordings.
360.q: At that time you had Fletcher Henderson and of course Duke. The Count hadn’t really come on to the scene at that time much. We heard a lot of Fats Waller from where he was broadcasting from — Cincinnati I think. I heard a lot of Fats Waller. And of course Coleman Hawkins, Ben Webster. And…

396.t: Her style on tenor, flute and baritone
396.s: She is not a bebopper; Royal Stokes called her a keeper of the flame, with Lester Young, Hawkins and Lucky Thompson on tenor, Latin on flute, lyrical baritone; they admire Nick Brignola and Pepper Adams.
396.q: I wish I were a bebopper. I really don’t have the language, you know, the way some people do. There might be hints of it in my playing. But my — in one book, Royal Stokes’ book, he put me in the chapter “keepers of the flame.” I guess that a lot of people find elements of Lester Young, Coleman…

678.s: Harry Carney as his idol, plus Cecil Payne, Pepper Adams, Brignola, Cuber, Smulyan and Gerry Mulligan.
678.ch: Baritone, other horns and the Lincoln Center band
678.q: Oh yeah, Ernie Caceres, and of course Harry Carney was always my idol. I really thought Harry Carney was the epitome of the sound of the baritone. I like other people. I like Cecil Payne, I’m very fond of Cecil Payne, and he’s a very good personal friend of mine. But I mean before that I was…

612.s: He enjoys differing musical ideas, admires Ben Webster and Hawkins, and recalls a 1976 Michael's Pub remark that his violin sounded like a horn.
612.q: Well I had a lot of fun because I played with a lot of different musicians and all of them, take three or four musicians, all of them play the same tune down, they all have different ideas. And one would be if it’s pretty to me it might not be pretty to you, but they play something else that’s…

366.t: Recording with Chubby Jackson and Coleman Hawkins; Hawkins with Henderson
366.s: Sol recalls Chubby Jackson, his Metropole-era album with Coleman Hawkins, and Hawkins in Henderson's band.
366.q: A very funny guy. Very, very humorous. He has a good attitude and he loves to play and a great player. I don’t use that word loosely. To me that word “great” Monk is a superlative. Benny Goodman, great. Louis Armstrong, great. Teddy Wilson, great. Art Tatum, great. Jess Stacy, piano, great. Mel…

503.s: Burrell admires Hawkins's quick ears and unique sound on the Bluesy Burrell session.
503.q: So I just called to do sessions with this great master and then I think they allowed me to do a date as a leader and he said yeah, he'd play with me. I think this was after I'd done a couple with him, but I was amazed--you know you hear the records and you hear about how great somebody is but then…

451.t: Playing with Coleman Hawkins and Hank Jones
451.s: Sessions with Hawkins; Hank Jones on an out-of-tune piano.
451.q: Yeah. I’m sure that Sonny Rollins thinks of that, you know. And I imagine Coleman Hawkins did, as well. (laughs) I actually played with Coleman Hawkins a couple times, just kind of jam sessions but…

225.s: Johnson worked and recorded with Hawkins a few times and remembers him as bright and personable.
225.q: Not a lot. On some few occasions, yes. I don’t even remember the details of those occasions. I just remember that I worked with "Bean", as we called him, a few times. It was an interesting experience to play with Coleman because he was such a brilliant saxophonist. His style was different from all…

372.s: He discusses Koller's playing, his falling out, and his paintings.
372.q: I think he was very sympathetic with that music overall, Warne also, of course. We were very close for some years and then he asked me to do a project and I couldn’t do it. I don’t think I wanted to do it, something else was up, and he seemed to turn against me, and Russo too who he was very close…

505.t: Sax Legends and Steve Coleman's master class
505.s: On a Japanese saxophone-legends record he heard Steve Coleman, who later gave the best presentation ever at Liebman's master class.
505.q: Yep. I’ll tell you about that date. I drove with Phil Woods, in fact the first time that I actually really talked to him. I drove him in. I recorded my track with Steve Coleman. Then I got – Steve was playing – I never heard Steve play next to me. Like I said, you learn more when you’re next to…

492.t: Coleman Hawkins's tenor left in the car on Central Avenue
492.s: Lloyd tells how Hawkins left his saxophone on the back seat in Los Angeles and no one touched it, as a measure of respect.
492.ch: Booker Little and the Manassas circle
492.q: So dig this: When I graduated from college - So Booker and I would stay close, he’d come out with Max, you know, once or twice a year or something. I want to interject something - bring me back to that, but this is very interesting because - Booker was staying in a hotel called the Adams Hotel over…

508.t: Coleman Hawkins humbling himself on The Hawk Flies High
508.s: Hawkins played a Parker solo late in life, which Sonny Rollins revered; he kept changing while Benny Carter stayed bitter.
508.q: Coleman Hawkins had that kind of…. Younger musicians had that kind of reverence for him. Sonny Rollins is, to this day, still in awe of Coleman Hawkins. Coleman had that thing…. There’s a great recording of Coleman Hawkins toward the end of his life doing this record. It’s not a very good record.…

100.t: Coleman Hawkins vouches for him; interviews with Milt Jackson and Roy Eldridge
100.s: Hawkins's drink initiation, the Milt Jackson interview, Eldridge checking him out, and writing A Night at Birdland.
100.ch: Metropole, Copper Rail and first jazz writing
100.q: my musician friends. But the fortunate thing was that he was recording for Atlantic, and Down Beat arranged for me to attend the session. He was recording with Coleman Hawkins, whom I had at that time already befriended. In fact, Coleman did a very big thing for me in terms of establishing me in…

705.t: Melba's arrangements arriving at the last minute: Hawkins and Montreal 1985
705.s: He recalls his idol Coleman Hawkins, the live 1959 Five Spot date, and the 1985 Montreal tour, when her music arrived despite hospital stays.
705.q: Spirit. It makes no difference where she was: North Pole, or the middle of the Congo, it makes no difference. A good example of that is this, when we did the date with Coleman Hawkins, which was another miracle for me because Coleman Hawkins was my idol. When “Body and Soul” came out I was 17 years…

63.t: First hearing Coleman Hawkins with Fletcher Henderson
63.s: Hawkins's sound and chord sense at the Roseland stood out from the band; Shaw also recalls Bix with Whiteman.
63.q: I think it was Fletcher [Henderson] at the Roseland Ballroom. I remember him. I remember Tricky Sam [Nanton]. I can’t remember a lot about that band. I didn’t . . . The band didn’t impress me much. But when the Hawk played, or Bean, as they called him, that was a whole new thing. He had great chord…

230.t: Johnny Hodges as influence, versus Charlie Parker
230.s: Barnet says Hodges, not Bechet, influenced him on alto and soprano, and would rather hear Hodges play a melody than Parker's acrobatics.
230.ch: Singers, Las Vegas, Hodges and road life
230.q: : Well, no, the question -- I was asked the question, how do you rate Johnny Hodges and Charlie Parker, and I said, 'I appreciate everything that Charlie Parker does.' If you know anything about music or saxophone playing at all you have to realize that this man was a giant. However, for my own…

26.t: Coleman Hawkins never cut the band; Hawk and Mamie Smith
26.s: Greer denies a battle story, recalls Hawkins with Mamie Smith, and compares Hawkins with Johnny Hodges.
26.q: No, never happened. Never happened. Hawk was at the top of the heap but he -- now, Hawk and I were, for many years -- when it was Mamie Smith.

17.ch: Broadway, tenors, Billie Holiday and Rhythm Club memories
17.q: That was another good car. Kirby and Hawk had, and I had one too. Yeah, a DeSalle, yeah that was it.

146.t: Why Lester had no imitators: Hawkins, Chu Berry, Ike Quebec
146.s: Everyone followed Hawkins and then Chu Berry; Hawkins cut Body and Soul to answer Berry, and Ike Quebec copied that solo.
146.q: Yeah, yeah. All of them were listening to Hawkins. And then Chu Berry come along, and they got behind Chu Berry. That's why Hawkins made that special chorus on "Body and Soul."

89.t: Mamie Smith as a person, and meeting fifteen-year-old Coleman Hawkins
89.s: He calls Mamie a shouter rather than a blues singer, then recounts a teenage Coleman Hawkins sitting in at Kansas City, never hitting a bad note in five years with Fletcher.
89.q: Mamie, in my mind, was what we called a shouter. She wasn't a blues singer like Bessie. Bessie was truly a blues singer. But Mamie was the first to record and naturally she would be the first one considered. She was a very fine looking woman, nice personality, easily led. She usually had a husband…

380.t: Coleman Hawkins as a kind man
380.s: He recounts a dream about Ben Webster and Hawkins and the thrill of Hawkins speaking to him as a kid.
380.ch: Youth, the road and arrival in California
380.q: Well, I had gotten to know Coleman Hawkins, you know, very briefly -- but what a beautiful human being he was. At least to me. He talked to me, and you know, being the kind of kid I was, I was just enthralled that he would speak to me. Because I used to stand in front of the

117.s: Hawkins, a loner, visits Freeman and says they are still in demand because they knew their instruments when young; Freeman calls Hawkins the father of tenor soloists.
117.q: Well, Red, of course, was always a fine musician. You know, people ask all the time, how does it happen that you can still play at this age and so on, well, I remember a few years before Coleman Hawkins died, I had an apartment in New York and he -- I didn't know this -- all these years was living…

383.t: Coleman Hawkins: genius, 'Body and Soul' and his philosophy
383.s: Wilson ranks Hawkins among a few geniuses, praises the continuity of 'Body and Soul', and relays Hawkins's belief that unplanned things matter most.
383.q: Yes, Coleman Hawkins was one of that little handful of very special, exceptionally talented people, Coleman Hawkins, Benny Carter, Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, Art Tatum, these few who are far superior to the others in their

92.t: Benny Carter's all-saxophone date: Hawkins outplays Phil Woods on 'Midnight Sun'
92.s: On a 1964 Carter date with five saxophones, Hawkins took the solo and amazed Phil Woods by playing the tune every which way.
92.ch: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
92.q: Yeah, he was. And Ben and Coleman Hawkins. But Hawk now, speaking of this same band, Phil Woods, they featured -- one of his featured numbers in Quincy's band was 'Midnight Sun Never Sets,' you know. What is that, 'the Midnight Sun.'

29.s: Willard says Hawkins came in 1923 with Mamie Smith and Harvey Brooks; Howard says he only tried to get a job and was scared by Hawkins's sound.
29.ch: Quality Serenaders, Cotton Club and union recollections
29.q: Yes, he was a very good player. Scared me to death with a horn, till I got in there, then it didn't scare me no more.

385.t: Coleman Hawkins as a fishing friend
385.s: Hawkins bought five hundred dollars of fishing gear, ran a miniature train set, and drove too fast.
385.ch: Chords, recordings and his own groups
385.q: Oh yeah we were good friends. He was one of the fellas that used to go fishin'. He'd go fishin'. Man I took him fishin' one time and the next time I know this cat had about 500 dollars worth of fishin' stuff & he didn't even know which way it go. . . . He had money. He had a hell of a train set. A…

169.s: McGhee followed Prez nightly and praised Hawkins' 'Body and Soul' nights.
169.ch: Writing, Oklahoma roots and the origins of bebop
169.q: Yeah, well, he was something else. But he sounded so beautiful, man, I don't know how anybody wouldn't want to do something for him, man. I remember I used to love to go... I used to go and hear that sound that was coming out of Minton's when Charlie would be there playing. Prez, too. I had to go…

149.s: Coleman liked Paul Bascomb's solo on 'Lost in the Shuffle' and they became friends.
149.ch: Highlights, the reunion album and fellow musicians
149.q: I was getting ready to bring up Coleman Hawkins. Ben Webster. So, I was, I would say Ben Webster was one I really liked besides Coleman Hawkins. Coleman Hawkins used to do different concerts with the small group in Long Island. He was, I don't know. I forgot how they advertised. It said the "Hawks"…

6.t: Coleman Hawkins and the shift from fast dance tempos to slow playing
6.s: He calls Hawkins the greatest saxophonist, describes sitting beside him and watching him develop, and explains that ballroom bands played fast until Hawkins brought slow playing.
6.ch: Jelly Roll's road trip, Benny Carter and Chick Webb
6.q: Oh, yes, yes, yes. Well, that was a great thing. Coleman Hawkins was one of the greatest. He was one of the greatest saxophone players because he had such a conception of playing the horn and he was a thorough musician, because he could play all the chords. He knew all the chords, you know, because…

97.t: Coleman Hawkins's lateness and Henderson's threats to fire him
97.s: Henderson threatens to fire Hawkins for arriving late, but the band pleads for him.
97.q: Well, Fletcher was a very -- he was a fellow that -- he was strict and nice and exact in everything he did. But he wasn't satisfied with his band. And he threatened to fire Coleman Hawkins more than once, because Coleman used to come in late. Sometimes we'd open up and start playing, and here comes…

125.t: Coleman Hawkins as a college of music
125.s: Thompson calls Hawkins and Tatum ultimate teachers, discusses Hawkins' return from Europe and ranks him with Lester Young as tenor leaders.
125.ch: New York with Lester Young and Coleman Hawkins
125.q: turer, wasn't he? I refer to Coleman Hawkins as a college of music, jazz music, any kind of music, jazz music in particular. Because that's the way -- but you can remember that I've met people like Art Tatum, and I put Coleman Hawkins in the same category. These people were what you call the…

78.t: Fletcher's rehearsals and conductor sheets; Hawkins in hard keys
78.s: Fletcher rehearsed thoroughly, sent conductor sheets for Goodman's band, and Hawkins played better the harder the key.
78.ch: Fletcher as a leader and early bandmates
78.q: He was pretty thorough at rehearsals because, even with his own band, they knew his style, you know, and it wasn't any hard thing to do, but just if he -- he would write skeleton things too, you know, and he would explain where to jump, and I wanted to insert this, but I didn't have time to do…

79.t: Bud Rankin's family and rehearsals at Moreau gigs
79.s: The Rankin family hosted rehearsals in their living room. Bud's father had the first taxicab in town. A violinist from St. Joe who worked with Coleman Hawkins joined the Moreau gigs.
79.q: Yeah. They were doing all right there and very well respected people. And he would call in a fellow from St. Joe and he played violin and he used to work with Coleman Hawkins and his-name-is and I can't think of his name offhand right now but I will sometime later on.
